what: What could be done about the full run under a spending cap of 50 US dollars in total, 2026-11-21. The owner set the cap at 50 that day, with 9.03 recorded as spent and a sixth rehearsal running. The launcher refuses a full run unless the cap covers recorded spend plus the run's worst case (2.00 USD per hour for the 42-hour maximum run time, 84 USD), so the run as designed could not start. Nine AI agents, all read-only: four each analysed one way forward (A as designed, B a Spot machine made resumable, C the 128 GB machine, D the Mac alone), four each checked one analysis independently and adversarially, and one looked for what was missing and ranked the options; that last agent also proposed further ways (its E to H), which no other agent checked. None of them ran anything in the cloud, and none decided anything: the choice is the owner's. Figures are as the agents gave them; where an analysis and its check differ, the check and the last agent's reading of the files are the ones to go by. Whole-tree hours are projections throughout.
the_question_put_to_each_agent: See 'option' in each analysis; the rules were: read only, no cloud commands, no build commands, blind to anyone else's results on this proof, every number traced to a file.

analysis.option: A: the full run as designed and rehearsed, on demand, on n4d-highmem-32 (one 440 GB Hyperdisk Balanced data disk at 6,000 IOPS and 300 MiB/s, plus a 50 GB Hyperdisk Balanced boot disk; leanchecker replay with import-closure directories; no second replay; GCP_KEEP_OLEANS=0)
analysis.summary: Option A does not fit a 50 USD total cap, in any case and on either price basis. The low case alone is 22.7 billed hours, which is 45.40 USD at the ledger's 2.00 rate (42.40 at the true list rate of 1.868 per hour). Add the 9.73 already spent or expected, and the final recorded spend is 55.13 in the low case, 60.93 expected and 76.73 high. Under a 50 cap with 9.73 spent, the most machine time affordable at 2.00 per hour is 20.1 hours (19.2 if the running rehearsal costs its 2.50 maximum). That is less than the low estimate, so no change to MAXRUN or to the rate constant can make a run that is able to finish fit under 50. For "launch full" to start exactly as written, the cap must be at least 9.73 + 84.00 = 93.73, or 95.53 if the rehearsal costs 2.50. The teardown can record up to 120 seconds past MAXRUN, so the recorded worst case is 84.07, not 84.00. Nothing is resumable: if the VM is deleted before the run finishes, the whole build is lost. A second attempt costs the whole amount again.

changes_needed: Nothing in code is needed to run option A. The owner would have to raise GCP_SPEND_CAP_USD in config.env to at least 93.73 (95.53 to cover a 2.50 rehearsal); 96 covers the recorded worst case of 95.60. No cap of 50 or below can work.

Optional, config only: set GCP_RATE_USD_PER_HOUR to 1.87, the true list rate of 1.868 rounded up. The worst case would fall from 84.00 to 78.54 (78.60 recorded with the 120 s), and the cap needed to 88.27 to 90.13. The ledger would then track the bill more closely, but it would keep no margin for tax, egress or bucket storage. None of this changes expected spend.

Optional, code: lower MAXRUN and DEADLINE_MIN (pilot_local.sh line 124; the comments in its header; cloud/gcp/README.md and docs/cloud-notes.md s.9 say 42 h). Keep the gap of at least 60 minutes between them, which the watchdog (600 s) and report wait (1,800 s) need. For example, 37 h / 2220 min gives a worst case of 74.00 and a cap of about 84. The code change needs a commit and a fresh 'stage', because launch refuses a dirty scripts/ or cloud/ and staged tools from another commit (lines 116-119). It cannot reach a MAXRUN of 20.1 h, which is what 50 would require.

If the owner wants the 50 cap kept, option A has to be refused rather than changed: a run cut to 20 h would end in the C3 short-cap path, with no criterion answered, and spend about 40 USD for nothing.
risks: Nothing is resumable. The build lives only on the VM's disks, and both auto-delete with the VM (pilot_local.sh line 125; --instance-termination-action=DELETE). Compiled files are uploaded only when full-keep-oleans=1, and even then only after every check has run (full_guest.sh lines 897-917): never before the deadline, and the full mode sets it to 0. The guest never runs twice on one VM (lines 343), and no script fetches earlier results to resume. A failed or cut-off run therefore costs the whole amount again, and the Mac's build may not seed it. Two attempts at expected cost come to about 102 USD at the ledger rate.

What does survive a deletion is in the bucket: status.json, heartbeat and the small logs every minute (sync_small, line 139); modules.tsv, system.tsv and the C3 results.tsv every ten minutes (sync_big, lines 140-144, 348); the build logs and c1_modules after the build; the seal manifests; the C2 outputs as each run ends; facts.json at each checkpoint. That is an account of how far the run got, not anything a new VM can build on.

Near its own deadline (41 h) the guest's watchdog signals the main script and kills the build tool, xargs, timeout, tar and zstd, unless a report is under way. After 600 s, or up to 1,800 s more if a report has begun, it uploads logs, the last checkpoint's facts and a DEADLINE status, then idles until deletion (full_guest.sh lines 352-371). At most a few minutes of C3 results are lost. Google deleting the VM early is not expected: the VM is STANDARD, not Spot. If it did happen, the loss would be up to ten minutes of replay results plus the final report.

If the replay trials find that leanchecker cannot cover the tree in the time left, the main pass is cut to C3_SHORT_CAP (3600 s) and the run ends without answering C3 (lines 822, 835-840). A smaller MAXRUN makes this more likely, and so does the unmeasured link cost.

Never rehearsed, by any run: the full-mode limits (2460/151200), the deadline and watchdog path, a full-size seal, C2 on the final theorem, the C3 retry passes, and (until the rehearsal now running) leanchecker with import-closure directories and hard links across users after fs.protected_hardlinks=0 (full-rehearsals/README.md, closing list; docs/cloud-notes.md s.9).

The hard-link cost is assumed at 60 microseconds per link. On the Mac, making the links alone cost about 0.5 ms per link plus about 0.4 s per check. If anything like that holds on the cloud machine, the replay grows by about 2-3 h (1.52 h per added second per check), which is about 5-6 USD more and pushes the high case to about 36 h.

The import-closure replay time is a projection from a two-point fit. Its listing term sits near the measured point (4.36 s with 12,244 files), but its closure term for the deepest modules is extrapolated: 27 modules import more than 50,000 others, and no module above 17,860 imports was ever compiled or checked in the cloud (docs/cloud-notes.md s.8.4).
A build failure or a stop at the restart tests ends the run early and cheaply, but gives no verification and needs a whole new run.

The ledger is an estimate. Tax, egress for downloading results, bucket storage and, at the 2.00 rate, nothing else fall outside it; the bill is authoritative. Because NOW is taken before create and teardown can lag, the recorded worst case is 84.07, so a cap set to exactly spent + 84.00 can be overshot by 0.07.
unknowns: The cost of making and removing the hard links on Linux XFS on Hyperdisk with 32 workers. The running rehearsal may give the first number on a shallow tree.
The leanchecker cost per check for modules with very large import closures, on the cloud machine.
Time and memory of C2, plain and deep, on the full tree (allowance 0.5 h expected, 2 h high).
The final cost of the rehearsal running now.
Whether N4D capacity is available in the configured zones when launching (the pilot found none in us-central1).
Tax and small charges (egress, bucket storage) on the real bill.

Whether the 50 GB boot disk is billed at the Hyperdisk Balanced default provisioning I read from Google's documentation (3,300 IOPS and 215 MiB/s, about 0.006 USD/h above baseline). I read the rates themselves from the repository's estimator, not from today's price page.
analysis.verdict: Option A cannot run under a 50 USD total cap. Even its low case comes to 55.13 recorded (52.13 at the true list rate), and expected is 60.93. To fit 50, a run would have to finish in at most 20.1 billed hours, and the low estimate is 22.7. Shrinking MAXRUN or the rate constant only lowers the bound the launcher checks; it cannot make a run that finishes affordable at 50, and below about 34 h it mostly adds the chance of paying for a run that ends at its deadline with nothing usable. For "launch full" to start unchanged, the cap must be at least 93.73 (95.53 if the rehearsal costs its 2.50 maximum). I would defend 96, since the ledger can record 84.07 for the run. Expected final recorded spend is about 61 USD (55 to 77, about 83 if the link cost is Mac-like). Every failed attempt costs the whole amount again, because nothing carries over to a new VM.

Watch is a foreground process on the Mac that must stay up for about 26 hours, and interrupting it in full mode only stops watching (pilot_local.sh line 190). Losing it turns an expected 51.20 into 84.07 recorded. This is the largest cost risk in option A, and the analysis does not mention it.
The recorded worst case of the running full-rehearsal is 2.57, not 2.50 (MAXRUN 4500 + 120 s at 2.00/h), so the 'at most' figures should be 11.60 / 95.60 / 95.67.

Three settings come from config.env, which I was not allowed to open: GCP_SECOND_REPLAY, GCP_KEEP_OLEANS and GCP_RATE_USD_PER_HOUR (pilot_local.sh lines 41, 46, 126). If GCP_SECOND_REPLAY=rhv-replay is set there, the run adds about 6 h, which is about 12 USD, and it goes against the owner's decision of no second replay. If GCP_KEEP_OLEANS=1 is set, the run ends with a tar and zstd of about 127 GB of compiled files, uploaded to gs://.../keep/. That costs extra machine time and also bucket storage that teardown never deletes (pilot_local.sh lines 256-258). A RATE other than 2.00 changes every cap figure. All three must be confirmed before launch.

The ephemeral external IPv4 address on the VM (no --no-address in the create command) is a cost left out of the 1.868/h list rate. docs/cloud-notes.md s.6 item 11 names it; I could not read its price from Google's page.
The low case has the same replay hours as expected (8.5), and it leaves out the 15 minutes of replay trials and the re-planning on each call. It is optimistic, not a floor.

The Mac record shows closure-directory checks at roughly 50-60 percent of whole-library cost, against about 35 percent from the fit. That is a second reason, beside the link cost, why the 5.6 s per check may be low. The 6,000-IOPS disk limit on link and unlink metadata is untested.

A VM restart (host error) ends the run: the guest sees its STARTED marker, reports FAIL and does nothing more (full_guest.sh line 343). Watch then tears it down. Nothing is resumable, and this is the same total loss as a deletion.
Teardown copies the results from the bucket before it deletes the VM (pilot_local.sh lines 235-239). That adds VM minutes on a full run, plus a little egress.

check.assessment:
The analysis is right on the main point. Option A does not fit a 50 USD total cap in any case: the low case alone records about 55. Its arithmetic checks out against the files. The rates in gcp_family_rates.json give 1.77888/h for the machine. The data disk and the 50 GB Hyperdisk Balanced boot disk add 0.07753/h and 0.01164/h, and Google's documented defaults of 3,300 IOPS and 215 MiB/s confirm the boot-disk figure. The hours 22.7 / 25.6 / 33.5 come from replay_cost.json. The launcher test is spent + 2.00 x 151200/3600 > cap, and teardown can record up to MAXRUN+120 s.

Its statements about resumability also hold. The disks auto-delete with the VM. The compiled files are uploaded only after every check, and only if keep-oleans is set. The guest refuses to run twice. What reaches the bucket (small logs every minute, results every ten minutes, facts at checkpoints) is an account of the run, not something a new VM can build on.

Three corrections matter:
1. The running full-rehearsal can record 2.57, not 2.50, so the 'at most' figures become 11.60 / 95.60 / 95.67.
2. Every expected figure assumes the local 'watch' process stays up for about 26 hours. The guest never shuts itself down, so without watch the VM runs to 42 h and records 84.07.
3. The suggested 1.87/h rate constant is not a safe ceiling once the external IPv4 address is counted. If the rate is lowered, use at least 1.88.

Also: the replay cost is a projection that has never been timed on the cloud machine, and the Mac data on link cost and closure-directory overhead points to it being low by about 2-4 h. Three settings in config.env (second replay, keep-oleans, rate) could not be checked, and one of them could go against the owner's no-second-replay decision. Measured: the spend records, the per-check costs at 1,792 and 29,633 compiled modules, the Mac link timings, and the prices. Projected: every whole-tree hour figure. Unknown: link and unlink throughput on Hyperdisk at 32 jobs, leanchecker cost for the deepest modules, C2 on the full tree, the live ledger's exact total, and the config.env overrides.

analysis.summary:
Spot cuts the machine part of the price from 1.779 to 1.014 USD/h. Disks are not discounted. With the 440 GB data disk and 50 GB boot disk, the all-in rate is 1.097 USD/h against 1.862 on demand. On the replay_cost.json hours (22.7 / 25.6 / 33.5), a run with no preemption costs 24.89 / 28.07 / 36.74 USD.

The driver as written cannot survive a preemption. The create command uses --instance-termination-action=DELETE and the data disk is auto-delete=yes, so a preemption deletes the VM and the whole build tree. Nothing but logs, status and the gzipped results.tsv has reached the bucket (keep-oleans=0 for full). The watch loop then sees the VM GONE (or TERMINATED/STOPPED) and runs teardown, which deletes every disk. A preemption at hour t costs about 1.10 x t USD and the run starts again from zero.

Switching to STOP does not rescue the current guest. On reboot, full_guest.sh line 343 sees /var/pilot/STARTED and refuses to run ("the run does not start twice"). s_disk would also mkfs.xfs -f the data disk. The seal deletes $AN, and with it the replay results, by design (line 664). iptables, sysctl and the mount do not persist across a reboot. DEADLINE and elapsed_s are measured from each boot. With STOP, the run-time limit also stops rather than deletes, so disks keep billing until teardown.

Resuming the build (lake reuses finished modules) and the replay (results.tsv kept, plan only what is owed) is possible in principle. It needs a re-entry design and at least 3 new Spot rehearsals that include forced interruptions.

Under the launcher's worst-case rule at 42 h, a Spot run needs a cap of about 57.7 USD (9.03 + 2.50 + 1.10 x 42), not 50. Under a 50 USD total cap, the room after the rehearsal now running is 38.47 USD in the worst case. That is enough at the expected run cost (about 28 USD plus about 0.5 to 1.1 USD per resumed restart, plus about 1.5 USD of Spot rehearsals). It is not enough at the high case with restarts. It also fits the launcher only if MAXRUN is cut to about 34 to 35 h, which leaves about 1 to 1.5 h of slack above the 33.5 h high case.

Google publishes no preemption rate for Spot VMs, for this family or any other. It says only that preemption is "generally low" and varies by day and zone.

analysis.cap_needed_usd: About 57.7 USD in total (9.03 recorded + 2.50 current rehearsal + 1.10 x 42 h), or about 59.2 counting about 1.5 USD of Spot rehearsals. At a ledger rate of 1.25 it is about 64. Keeping the 2.00 ledger rate would need 95.53. To fit a 50 USD total cap under the launcher's rule, MAXRUN must drop to about 34 to 35 h at a rate of 1.10, which leaves only about 1 to 1.5 h above the 33.5 h high case.
analysis.expected_additional_spend_usd: About 29 to 33 USD expected: the run 28.07 with no preemption, plus about 0.5 to 1.1 per resumed restart, plus about 1.1 to 2.5 for 3 to 5 Spot rehearsals. Low about 26. High about 40 to 42 (33.5 h plus two restarts plus rehearsals). With the driver as written, any preemption late in the run roughly doubles the run's cost.
analysis.hours_or_days_expected: About 26 h of machine time (22.7 to 33.5 h projected), plus 0.3 to 1 h per preemption and any wait for Spot capacity in the same zone, so 1 to 2 days of elapsed time. Before that: developing the resume changes (probably a day or more of work and review) and 3 to 5 Spot rehearsals of about 20 to 30 minutes each.
changes_needed: pilot_local.sh create: --provisioning-model=SPOT, and set GCP_RATE_USD_PER_HOUR to a Spot rate (at least 1.10; 1.0966 is the computed all-in rate and can change daily).

Choose one of two survival models. (a) --instance-termination-action=STOP, with the data disk left as it is: the VM and both disks survive a preemption, but the run-time limit then also stops instead of deleting, so disks bill about 2 USD/day until teardown. (b) Keep DELETE, but create the data disk separately with auto-delete=no and attach it with --disk name=... instead of --create-disk: a preemption deletes only the VM and boot disk, and the controller re-creates the VM in the same zone with the existing data disk. Either way the safety rule 'Google deletes everything at the limit' (pilot_local.sh header point 2) no longer holds for the disks.

Replace --max-run-duration with an absolute --termination-time set once at first launch (the duration resets on every restart; Google's limit-vm-runtime page). Re-create or restart only while that time is in the future.

Who restarts: the local watch loop (lines 194-228) must stop treating TERMINATED/STOPPED/GONE as the end. It should check whether the VM was preempted, then restart it with 'instances start' (model a) or re-create it (model b), retrying while there is no capacity, and tear down only on a final guest state or at the absolute deadline. A restart is only possible in the disk's zone. If the Mac is asleep or offline, nothing restarts the VM, and the disks keep billing. A Google-side restarter (for example a managed instance group with a stateful disk) would be a larger change and needs its own review.

Guest re-entry, line 343: replace 'never run twice' with a resume path keyed on markers on the data disk (model b) or boot disk (model a). Skip mkfs (line 382) when the filesystem holds a run with the same runtag, tarball SHA and guest SHA. Re-mount. Re-apply sysctl (max_map_count, file-max, nr_open, protected_hardlinks=0) and every iptables rule (pilot metadata block and lockdown, chk2/chk3 no_network) BEFORE any unprivileged process can run, and verify them as setup does. Check that no pilot/chk2/chk3 process exists. Re-verify toolchain, pkgs and source manifests against the stored baselines (setup steps are not redone; the stored baseline_*.txt are the reference).

Build resume: if interrupted in the build phase, restart lake (it reuses finished modules; lake restart measured at 4 to 9 s). Carry TESTS_DONE and the restart-test results across boots. Decide whether an unplanned restart's recompile count is recorded like the planned tests. Leave the .olean.tmp leftovers to the seal, as now. Add a check that compiled files written just before a hard power-off are not truncated, for example compare each .olean with its Lake .hash, or fsync/sync regularly.

Seal resume: if interrupted before SEALED was written, redo the whole seal. After SEALED, do NOT redo the rm -rf of $LOGS/$AN (line 664), which would erase the replay results. Instead re-hash the compiled files against lib_sha256.txt and the /opt/lean-tc copy against baseline_tc.txt, fail on any difference, re-check ownership and permissions, then continue. This keeps the anti-planting property only if nothing but root and the checkers touched the disk between boots, which must be argued and reviewed.
C2: re-run whichever axiom-check run was cut off (its outputs are taken only if newer than the c2_start marker). Persist C2_DEEP_WHEN and the results already obtained.

C3: persist the trial rate (C3_RATE, CHECK_JOBS, C3_FITS) and skip the trials on resume. Clear the stale run.lock that 09_kernel_replay.sh leaves after a kill ('a second run ... stops with an error'). Resume with the planner, which already keeps every result and plans only what is owed. Recompute C3_FITS from the absolute deadline.

Deadlines and accounting: pass an absolute deadline epoch in metadata in place of pilot-deadline-min. Keep run-start T0 from metadata. Record boot count, each boot's start and end, and the seconds lost per preemption in facts.json, phases.tsv and status.json. elapsed_s is currently per boot.

Signals: on the preemption shutdown, the TERM trap runs finish FAIL 'unexpected signal' (line 336), which uploads a final FAIL status, and watch would then tear down. Check the metadata 'preempted' flag and upload a PREEMPTED (non-final) status instead. Optionally set a 120 s preemption notice.

Ledger and cap: model a keeps one ledger row across restarts; its elapsed time includes stopped periods (conservative). Model b would need one row spanning re-creations, or the open-run check (line 107) blocks relaunch. Either way the cap check must use the Spot rate, the absolute termination time and a disk-only allowance after the VM is gone. Teardown must still positively verify that no disk is left.

Rehearsals before trusting it: at least 3 on Spot, about 0.35 to 0.5 USD each. (1) A clean run with the new flags and re-entry code. (2) An interruption forced during the build, resumed, showing no recompiled finished module and a clean seal. (3) An interruption forced during the C3 replay, resumed, showing results kept, no module counted twice and a correct summary. Preferably 2 more: interruptions during the seal and during C2 or the report, and the 'no capacity on restart' path. A user-forced stop is only a proxy for a real preemption: whether Google lets a user trigger a true Spot preemption was not checked.
risks: No published preemption rate. Over about 26 h on one Spot VM, the number of preemptions cannot be estimated from Google's own guidance. Several preemptions would erase the saving and, under a 50 USD cap, stop the run.

Capacity: on 2026-11-20 none of the four us-central1 zones had n4d-highmem-32 (docs/cloud-notes.md section 8). After a preemption, the VM can only be restarted in the data disk's zone. A long wait costs about 2 USD/day of disk, and nothing restarts it while the Mac is offline.

With STOP, the run-time limit also stops instead of deleting, and a stopped VM is apparently not acted on at its termination time (Google's page says a restart fails if the time has passed). Disks then bill until a person runs teardown, which breaks the current design's guarantee.
Spot prices can change up to once a day. A ledger rate of 1.10 has only 0.3 percent headroom over the computed 1.0966.
The pilot ran in us-east1-b; all rates in the records are us-central1.

A hard power-off after a 0 to 30 s notice may leave partly written or zero-length compiled files on XFS. Whether Lake would then treat such a module as finished is unknown. The kernel replay would probably record a failure or 'could not open', which would need diagnosis.

Resuming after the seal weakens the separation argument: it must be shown that nothing outside root and the checkers can touch the disk between boots, and that re-hashing is a sufficient re-seal. This needs fresh review on top of the five reviews already done.

The re-entry code is a substantial change to a driver whose current form (import-closure replay) has itself not yet been rehearsed. Each review-and-rehearse cycle costs time and some of the remaining 38 to 40 USD.

If the expected case slips toward the high case (33.5 h), the 34 to 35 h MAXRUN that fits the cap leaves no room for a restart. The guest would then cut the replay short (C3_FITS false, one-hour short pass), and the run would not settle criterion C3.
unknowns: Google's Spot preemption probability for N4D in the chosen zones over about 26 h: not published.
Today's N4D Spot rates. Google's Spot price page was too large to fetch, so the records' 2026-11-20 us-central1 rates are unconfirmed for today and for us-east1.
Whether a STOPPED Spot VM is deleted, or ignored, when its termination-time passes. Read from Google's page as not acted on, but not stated directly.
Whether a true Spot preemption can be triggered for a rehearsal, as opposed to a user stop.
Time to re-hash about 127 GB of compiled files after a reboot with a cold page cache: about 7 minutes if disk-bound at 300 MiB/s (projection only).
Whether Lake detects a truncated output after a hard power-off.
Full-scale durations of the seal, the C2 deep walk and the import-closure replay on a rented machine; none has been run on the full tree.
The cost of the rehearsal now running (at most 2.50 USD).
analysis.verdict:
Spot cannot simply be switched on. With the driver as written, a preemption loses everything: the VM is deleted, its data disk goes with it, and watch then runs teardown, which deletes every disk. Getting through a preemption needs new code: re-entry into the guest script, a restart step in watch, an absolute termination time, and a rule for the seal that does not erase replay results on resume. That needs review and at least 3 Spot rehearsals that include forced interruptions.

Once those changes exist, the expected cost is about 28 USD for the run plus about 0.5 to 1.1 USD per restart and about 1.5 USD of rehearsals. That fits the roughly 38.5 USD left under a 50 USD total cap. The high case with two restarts (about 38 to 40 USD plus rehearsals) does not fit.

The launcher's worst-case rule also does not fit at 42 h. It needs a cap of about 57.7 USD at a ledger rate of 1.10, or MAXRUN cut to about 35 h, which leaves almost no slack above the 33.5 h high case. So a full Spot run fits 50 USD only with changes, and only if the run lands near the expected case with at most one or two cheap restarts. One or two restarts fit only in the expected case, not in the high case.

corrections.claim: Longest MAXRUN that fits 38.47 USD is 34.97 h at RATE 1.10, leaving about 1 to 1.5 h of slack above the 33.5 h high case
corrections.finding: This leaves out two things. (1) The analysis itself requires 3 to 5 Spot rehearsals, and those come out of the same 38.47 USD before the full run is launched. (2) The guest's deadline sits an hour inside MAXRUN: the guest stops at 2,460 min against 2,520 min. The guest also holds back FINAL_RESERVE, 1,500 s by default, when it decides whether the replay fits (C3_FITS, line 822). After about 1.5 USD of rehearsals the room is 36.97 USD, so MAXRUN is 33.6 h and the guest's deadline about 32.6 h. That is below the 33.5 h high case, not 1 to 1.5 h above it. Even with no rehearsals, 34.97 h gives a guest deadline of 33.97 h, which is about 0.5 h above the high case, not 1 to 1.5 h.
corrections.corrected_value: MAXRUN = (38.47 - rehearsals) / 1.10: 33.6 h with 1.5 USD of rehearsals, 32.7 h with 2.5 USD. The guest's deadline is 1 h less than that, and the replay-fit test keeps back a further 25 min. In the high case nothing is left for a restart, and the high case itself may not fit.
corrections.source: cloud/gcp/pilot_local.sh lines 124 and 151-152; cloud/gcp/full_guest.sh lines 87, 97 and 822; records/cloud/replay_cost.json whole_run, import-closure high case 33.5 h

corrections.claim: Model (b), keeping DELETE with the data disk set to auto-delete=no: guest re-entry re-verifies against the stored baseline_*.txt, and setup steps are not redone
corrections.finding: Under model (b) the boot disk is deleted at each preemption, and with it everything the guest keeps there. That includes /var/pilot ($PD): baseline_src.txt, baseline_tc.txt, baseline_pkgs.txt, STARTED, SEALED, lib_sha256.txt after the seal, the c2 results and the copied build logs. It also includes the elan toolchain under the build user's home directory (.elan), /opt/rhv (the tools), /opt/lean-tc, the pilot, chk2 and chk3 users, cron.deny and limits.d. baseline_src.txt is never uploaded at all. baseline_tc and baseline_pkgs go to the bucket only at the seal (line 735). So a re-created VM has to redo setup, including downloading the toolchain again from the network, and the records taken before the first compile would be gone unless $PD is moved to a root-only directory on the data disk. Ownership of the files on the data disk also depends on the re-created users getting the same UIDs.
corrections.corrected_value: Model (b) needs a re-setup path, and $PD has to be moved onto the data disk in a root-only directory. Without both, the seal's comparisons cannot be made after a preemption during the build. Model (a), STOP, keeps the boot disk, and the claim holds only for model (a).
corrections.source: cloud/gcp/full_guest.sh lines 65, 98, 377, 391-398, 408, 413, 420-422, 663 and 735; cloud/gcp/pilot_local.sh line 162 (boot disk created with the VM)

corrections.claim: C3 resume must clear the stale run.lock that 09_kernel_replay.sh leaves after a kill ('a second run ... stops with an error')
corrections.finding: This is not upheld. The script takes over a lock whose process is gone, or is no longer this script (lines 154-173). It stops with an error only if a live 09_kernel_replay process holds the lock.
corrections.corrected_value: No lock clearing is needed. A guard directory, run.lock.takeover, left by a start killed at that exact moment is removed after a minute.
corrections.source: scripts/09_kernel_replay.sh lines 154-178

corrections.claim: On preemption the TERM trap runs finish FAIL 'unexpected signal', which uploads a final FAIL status
corrections.finding: The trap is there (line 336), but finish() calls report() before it uploads the status. report() runs c3_summary under timeout 900, put_logs and several uploads, retried up to 3 times, and only then calls status (lines 325-327). Google's preemption shutdown is best effort and at most 30 s. The FAIL status will most likely never be uploaded. watch would then end on GONE (DELETE) or on TERMINATED/STOPPED (STOP), not on FAIL. The outcome is the same either way: teardown.
corrections.corrected_value: The final status after a preemption is probably not uploaded. watch tears down on the VM state, not on a guest FAIL.
corrections.source: cloud/gcp/full_guest.sh lines 306-330 and 336; docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/spot ('best effort and up to 30 seconds', read 2026-11-21)

corrections.claim: With the driver as written, any preemption late in the run roughly doubles the run's cost
corrections.finding: Under a 50 USD total cap a second attempt is usually impossible, so a preemption does not double the cost: it ends the attempt. Relaunching with MAXRUN M at 1.10 USD/h needs 1.10 x M <= 38.47 - 1.10 x t, where t is the hours lost. With M = 33.5 h that means t <= 1.5 h. With M = 27 h it means t <= 8 h. At the 42 h MAXRUN no relaunch fits at all.
corrections.corrected_value: As written, one preemption after the first hour or two ends the full run under the 50 USD cap. About 1.10 USD per hour elapsed is lost, and nothing can be relaunched.
corrections.source: cloud/gcp/pilot_local.sh lines 107, 151-152 and 213-214

corrections.claim: Whether a true Spot preemption can be triggered for a rehearsal was not checked (listed as unknown)
corrections.finding: Google's Spot page now answers this. It says a preemption can be simulated by stopping or deleting the VM. It does not describe any way to trigger a real preemption.
corrections.corrected_value: A rehearsal can only use a user stop or delete as a proxy. A real ACPI soft-off preemption notice cannot be rehearsed on demand, by Google's documentation.
corrections.source: docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/spot (read 2026-11-21)

missed: The present driver, with import-closure leanchecker and fs.protected_hardlinks=0, has never been rehearsed: records/cloud/full-rehearsals/README.md says so, and docs/cloud-notes.md section 9 says so. The 8.5 h replay is a projection (replay_cost.json, whole_tree note). Spot adds re-entry code on top of a driver that is itself unrehearsed, so every rehearsal has to test both.

The rehearsals with forced interruptions will run longer than the five past ones (872 to 1,216 s). They include a stop, a restart and a resume, so about 30 to 40 min each, or about 0.55 to 0.75 USD at 1.10 USD/h, not 0.36. Three to five of them come to about 1.2 to 3.0 USD, all from the same 38.47 USD.

Legacy preemptible VMs are always stopped after 24 hours (Google's preemptible page). A run of about 26 h must use --provisioning-model=SPOT, not --preemptible. The analysis names SPOT but does not say why it matters.

Spot VMs cannot live-migrate (Google's Spot page). A host maintenance event therefore adds to the interruption risk on top of capacity preemptions. Whether such events terminate N4D Spot VMs was not confirmed here.

If the Spot VM is restarted later, the wait is wall-clock time against an absolute termination time. Under model (a) a long wait for capacity uses up the run's own time budget, as well as costing about 2 USD/day for the disks. It can push the replay into C3_FITS=0 (a one-hour short pass), and C3 would then not be settled.

The ledger prices machine time at 2.00 USD/h against a true list rate of about 1.862, so the recorded 9.03 USD overstates list spend by about 7 percent (about 8.4 at 1.862). Nothing in the files says whether the owner's 50 USD cap counts the ledger or the bill. The difference, about 0.6 USD, matters only at the margin.

No resumable design has been written or reviewed. Five rounds of review cover the current driver (docs/cloud-notes.md section 9), and the anti-planting argument at the seal would need a fresh review for any resume after the seal. That cost in time, and in further rehearsals, is not priced.
rule_conflicts: No conflict with the owner's decisions as stated: Spot keeps leanchecker with import-closure directories, needs no second replay, no Mac seed, no quota request (Spot uses standard quota while preemptible quota has never been requested) and no edit to PREREGISTRATION.md.
Asking for preemptible quota would be a quota request and is one-way (records/cloud/gcp_pricing.json quota finding 4). The plan must not do it, and the analysis correctly does not.

Model (a) (termination action STOP) removes the safety guarantee in the pilot_local.sh header, point 2, that Google deletes everything at the time limit. The run-time limit would then only stop the VM, and the disks would keep billing until a person runs teardown. That is a change to the agreed cost-bounding design, and it needs the owner's explicit agreement.

To stay inside 50 USD in total, MAXRUN must be about 32.7 to 33.6 h. The guest's deadline is then about 31.7 to 32.6 h, below the 33.5 h high case.

The run is 24.89 / 28.07 / 36.74 USD (low / expected / high) with no preemption: 1.0966 USD/h times 22.7 / 25.6 / 33.5 h. That rate is upheld from gcp_family_rates.json and gcp_pricing.json. Add about 0.33 to 1.10 USD per resumed restart plus disk time while waiting, and about 1.2 to 3.0 USD of rehearsals. Expected total is about 30 to 33 USD. check.assessment:
I upheld most of the other agent's analysis. Most of its numbers check out against the files they cite:
- **Rates:** Spot 0.01658 per vCPU-h and 0.001887 per GiB-h for the machine (1.0136 USD/h), and 0.0830 USD/h for the disks. The all-in rate is 1.0966 Spot against 1.862 on demand.
- **Hours and spend:** replay_cost.json gives 22.7 / 25.6 / 33.5 billed hours. Recorded spend is 9.03 (ledger 6.39 plus rehearsals 2.64). The launcher's worst case is RATE x MAXRUN (line 151).
- **Preemption with the driver as written:** the create command sets DELETE and auto-delete=yes (lines 125 and 161), watch ends on GONE or TERMINATED (lines 213-214) and runs teardown. On a reboot the guest refuses to run again (line 343), and the seal's rm -rf of $AN (line 664) would erase the replay results.
- **Google's documentation:** on 2026-11-21 it gives no preemption rate ("generally low"), Spot uses standard quota while preemptible quota has never been requested, Spot prices can change once a day, and the shutdown is best effort up to 30 s.

What I did not uphold, or found missing:
1. **The fit to the cap is too optimistic.** The MAXRUN that fits 50 USD ignores the Spot rehearsals the analysis itself requires, and the guest's deadline is an hour inside MAXRUN. With rehearsals included the guest's deadline comes out below the 33.5 h high case, not 1 to 1.5 h above it.
2. **Model (b) loses the boot disk.** That disk holds /var/pilot with the records taken before the first compile, the toolchain, the tools and the users. So setup would have to be redone, and the seal's comparisons would be impossible unless $PD moves to the data disk.
3. **The stale-lock fix is not needed.** 09_kernel_replay.sh already takes over a lock whose process is gone.
4. **The FAIL status probably never gets uploaded on preemption.** report() runs before status() and cannot finish in 30 s.
5. **A preemption does not double the cost, it ends the attempt.** Under a 50 USD cap a preemption with the driver as written leaves no room to relaunch.
6. **A real preemption cannot be rehearsed.** Google says to simulate one by stopping or deleting the VM.

Bottom line: Spot fits 50 USD only after new, reviewed resume code and several rehearsals. Even then it fits only near the expected case, with MAXRUN around 33 h, and the high case does not fit.

analysis.summary:
The memory need is set by file pages shared between processes, not by private memory. Private memory is small. In the pilot, compiler processes used a median of 504 MiB (fit: 508 MiB + 13 KiB per imported module, so about 2.7 GiB for the last module), and the whole machine never used more than 21.7 GiB of private memory. Checker processes used a median of 232 MiB (my fit: 225 MB + 0.010 MB per imported module). Each process also maps and touches compiled files: 6.4 GiB of libraries plus about 0.55 to 0.57 MiB per imported project module. The checker's own fit is 6,539 MB + 0.539 MB per import, almost the same as the compiler's. Projected to the whole tree, the touched set is about 98 GiB of project files plus 6.4 GiB of libraries, about 104 GiB. That is less than the 127 GB of compiled output on disk, because .ilean and other files are not touched. A 128 GB guest should see about 125 GiB (the pilot saw 251 of 256). After the OS and 11 to 35 GiB of private memory, about 90 to 113 GiB is left for page cache. So the whole touched set fits with a margin of a few GiB to a little over 10 GiB, or falls short by a similar amount. The pilot cannot tell which: it read only 2 MB from disk in 2 h 55 min, so there is no measurement of behaviour under memory pressure.

The import-closure replay does not change this picture. The hard links are the same inodes, so they share the same page cache. Each checker maps its closure, which it would map anyway. The only addition is 32 Python closure-worker processes, each holding the import graph, which I guess at about 0.1 to 0.2 GiB each (not measured).

Using the import graph, I estimated how much a short cache would hurt the random-order replay. A random 3,000-module window, about 9 minutes of replay, touches about 71 to 76 GiB. The coldest 30 percent of modules carry only 0.8 percent of import traffic. So even a cache 10 to 30 percent short of the tree would add only about 5 to 16 MB of disk reads per check, roughly 30 to 90 MB/s at 5.7 checks per second. The 300 MiB/s disk can serve that if page faults read about 128 KiB at a time. If they read 4 KiB at a time, 6,000 IOPS gives only about 23 MiB/s. The replay therefore looks robust.

The build is most exposed at the narrow top of the graph: 27 modules import more than 50,000 others and 13 more than 100,000, and each of those touches up to about 104 GiB. These run a few at a time, so private memory is low then and the set should just fit. There are also fixed extra reads: the seal and the end check hash 127 GB that is no longer in cache, about 6.7 minutes each, and the replay's cache warm-up takes about 6 minutes. The C2 deep walk, whose memory is unknown, would have only 15 to 20 GiB of headroom instead of about 150.

Running out of memory is unlikely. Private memory is far below RAM, and file pages can be reclaimed, so pressure shows up as slowdown from repeated disk reads rather than kills. In the replay, a kill (status 137) is recorded as not yet checked and costs only time. In the build, killed compilers force a second pass at 16 jobs; if they recur, the run ends BUILD_FAILED with no C1 result.

My estimate is 0.3 to 3.5 extra hours, about 1 hour likely. The tail is +10 hours if reads are small and the cache is short at the top, which would run past the 41-hour guest stop and leave C3 incomplete. Billed hours: about 23.0, 26.6 and 37.0 (low, likely, high), plus a 6-hour allowance for keeping the disks after the run. Cost on demand at 1.438 USD/h all-in: 33.6, 38.8 and 53.7 USD. Cost on Spot at 0.855 USD/h: 20.2, 23.2 and 32.1 USD, plus the risk of being preempted, which with termination action DELETE and auto-deleted disks loses the whole run.

Quota is the same as for the machine already granted: 32 vCPUs and 490 GB of Hyperdisk. Capacity for n4d-standard-32 by zone was not checked.

The launcher's worst case is RATE × 42 h. On demand with RATE set to 1.45, that is 60.90 USD, so the cap would need to be 72.43 USD; it does not fit 50. On Spot with RATE 0.86 to 0.90, the worst case is 36.12 to 37.80 USD, so the cap would need to be 47.65 to 49.33 USD. That fits 50 dollars total, but leaves no money for a second attempt or a calibration test, and it needs a code change to the provisioning model.

analysis.verdict:
Option C on demand does not fit a 50 USD total cap. The launcher would need a cap of 72.43 USD, and no sound shorter time limit fits. Option C on Spot fits on paper (cap 47.65-49.33 USD) and is the cheapest full run in the records, about 23 USD expected. It needs a committed change to the provisioning model, it is a single attempt that a preemption destroys, and it leaves no money for any calibration run first.

The memory analysis supports trying it. Private memory is small. The import-closure replay adds nothing to the page cache, since hard links share pages. The random replay barely suffers even if 10 to 30 percent of the tree is evicted. The expected penalty is about 1 hour, with a range of 0.3 to 3.5. The weak spots are the straight-line projection of the 104 GiB touched set, the top of the build and the C2 deep walk, none of which any test so far has reached.

No cheap test settles whether the whole tree fits, because only a near-full build creates that pressure, and uploading the Mac build is ruled out. A test can bound how much slower a cache miss makes things. The cheapest such test would run the pilot's deep build target under artificially reduced memory, with huge pages reserved or the run capped by memory cgroups, so that cache is short by a set fraction of the working set. That would take about 1 to 3 hours on n4d-standard-32, about 1.5 to 4.3 USD actual or 2 to 6 USD at the ledger's 2.00 rate, and needs a new guest mode. After about 2 USD of it, the Spot full run would still fit, barely: 11.53 + 2 + 36.12 = 49.65 USD. Anything more would not.

missed: The pilot's page cache reached 186 GiB (pilot_estimate.json memory.whole_machine.most_cached_gb), though it built only 17 percent of the tree. Its 'nothing read from disk' result depended on far more cache than a 128 GB guest has. Most of that cache was written files (setup files are 5.53 MB per module, 164 GB in the pilot, disk.txt setup_json_bytes). In a full run those writes, about 1.07 TB with setup files pruned every 600 s (full_guest.sh PRUNE_EVERY), pass through the same cache and compete with the compiled files the processes have mapped. The agent's cache budget leaves them out.

The C2 plain axiom check also imports the whole proof (the Lean frontend on a file that imports the final theorem), so it too needs about 104 GiB mapped plus its own memory. Each C2 run is limited to C2_TIMEOUT=7200 s (full_guest.sh line 84). If thrashing makes either C2 run time out, criterion C2 has no result. This is a failure, not just a slowdown, and costs up to 2 h each.

The import-closure replay makes about 175,187 x ~2,950 = ~5e8 hard links and the matching directories on the data disk (rhv_tools.py cmd_closure_worker; os.makedirs and os.link per file, rmtree after each module). That means dentry and inode slab memory and ext4 metadata writes that compete for the same cache and the same 6,000 IOPS / 300 MiB/s. It has not been rehearsed on a rented machine (cloud-notes 9, 'None of that last change has been rehearsed'), so its cost on either machine is unknown.

Each closure worker reloads the import graph for every batch of 25 modules (09_kernel_replay.sh BATCH=25, xargs -n 1 per batch), about 7,000 loads. That raises peak memory per worker and adds CPU that no estimate includes.

Ledger versus bill. The cap is enforced only on the ledger (RATE x seconds), not on Google's bill. Past rows are recorded at 2.00/h against about 1.86 actual, which overstates the 9.03 by about 0.6. A Spot run recorded at a fixed RATE understates the bill if the Spot price in the zone used is higher than the us-central1 rate on file. With a 50 USD total cap and 0.6-2.3 USD of margin, that difference matters.

Capacity cannot be checked from the records. gcp_machine_types.csv lists only machine types with at least 96 vCPUs (records/cloud/README.md), so it says nothing about where n4d-standard-32 is offered or has capacity.

Under Spot, Google's default preemption notice is 0 s (120 s can be requested), and with DELETE nothing survives. The guest's final status and facts.json from the last checkpoint may not upload. The run then ends with only what was already in the bucket.

The agent's figures for the top of the graph (27 modules above 50,000 imports, 13 above 100,000) come from cloud-notes 8.4 (reviewers' exact count), not from closure_stats.json. Its 1,500-module sample has a maximum of 49,768, and its key_module_closures lists five modules above 50,000. The figures are fine; the citation was partly wrong.
8.2's n4d-standard-32 rows (41/45/57 on demand, 25/27/34 Spot) are built on the superseded 14 h replay. The agent rebased onto 8.5 correctly, but anyone reading 8.2 alone would get the wrong numbers.

It does need a committed code change under cloud/ (--provisioning-model=SPOT in place of the hard-coded STANDARD), a fresh 'stage' (launch full refuses uncommitted files or a stale rhv_tools.id), and owner edits to config.env (GCP_MACHINE_TYPE, GCP_RATE_USD_PER_HOUR, GCP_SPEND_CAP_USD). check.assessment:
Mostly upheld in structure. Option C on demand cannot fit a 50 USD total under the launcher's rule, and on Spot it fits only on paper. But the margin is thinner than stated, and the time penalty figures are not supported by any record.

What I re-derived and uphold:
- Prices: 1.3552 on demand, 0.7721 Spot and 0.083 disks per hour (us-central1).
- The launcher's rule: WORST = RATE x 151,200 s; provisioning is hard-coded STANDARD; DELETE; auto-delete disks; 440 GB / 6,000 IOPS / 300 MiB/s data disk.
- Private memory per process is small; hard links share the page cache.
- Whole-tree touched set: 104 GiB at 0.572 MiB per module, or 124 GiB at the full 0.72 MB.
- A 3,000-module replay window touches about 75 GiB, and the cold tail carries almost no import traffic.
- Quota: Google confirms Spot uses standard quota, and that max-run-duration and DELETE work with Spot.

What I correct:
- The running rehearsal can record up to 2.57, not 2.50, because close_run caps at MAXRUN+120 s. Every cap figure moves by 0.07: Spot needs 47.72 (RATE 0.86) or 49.40 (RATE 0.90).
- The room left for a calibration test before the Spot run is at most 2.28 USD (RATE 0.86) or 0.60 (RATE 0.90), not 'about 2'.
- The +0.3 / +1.0 / +3.5 / +10 h penalty and the 23.0 / 26.6 / 37.0 h figures cannot be traced to any measurement; I do not uphold them. The pilot read nothing from disk and had up to 186 GiB of page cache.
- The agent's cache budget leaves out written files (about 1.07 TB of setup files pass through the cache), dentry and inode memory from about 5e8 hard links, and worker memory that may be up to 0.5 GiB each.
- Its tail case understates the failure modes. Both C2 runs import the whole proof under a 2 h timeout each, and real thrash ends the run at the deadline rather than adding a bounded 10 h.

Other points the decision depends on:
- Spot pricing is per region and can change daily. The rates on file are us-central1, while capacity was found in us-east1.
- The cap is enforced on the ledger, not on the bill.
- Capacity for n4d-standard-32 cannot be checked from the records.

Net: Spot Option C is feasible under 50 USD only as a single unrehearsed attempt, with 0.6 to 2.3 USD of ledger margin. A preemption or a thrash-induced deadline yields no C3 and leaves no money for a rerun.

analysis.summary:
Option D is allowed by the pre-registration and costs nothing more in the cloud. Spend stays at the recorded 9.03 USD plus at most 2.50 for the rehearsal now running.

(1) Preregistration. PREREGISTRATION.md line 66 says: "What may vary. The machine, the operating system, the number of parallel jobs, the per-process thread count, and where files are stored." C1 (line 48), C2 (lines 50-56) and C3 (line 60, "Every compiled module of the project is re-checked by `leanchecker` from the pinned toolchain, and every module passes.") all name tools and conditions, not machines, so all three can be met on the Mac alone. What is given up is S3, line 107: "Reproduce C1 to C3 on a second platform (a different operating system and processor architecture)." The cloud run would have been Linux on x86-64, so a Mac-only result is one platform. S1 (line 105) and S4 (line 108) are not affected; S2 (line 106) was already ruled out by the owner. Two rules bind harder on a 24 GB machine:
- Line 70: "A module whose compiler process is killed by the operating system for lack of memory ... has not been tested; it is re-run. A module is recorded as failing only when it fails with a Lean error, reproducibly, on a re-run with enough memory."
- Line 84: "The build cannot be completed with the resources available | INCONCLUSIVE".
If the last modules cannot be built in 24 GB, a Mac-only path ends INCONCLUSIVE, or needs another machine. Seeding a cloud machine from the Mac build is ruled out, so that would mean a full cloud rebuild.

A correction to the premise: the Mac has not been building "for days". The first START line in records/mac-build/build-status.txt is 2026-11-20 10:18 CST, and the 8-job run began at 14:18. At the last snapshot (09:31 CST, 15:31Z, 2026-11-21) it had been running about 23 hours: 59,988 of 175,187 modules compiled, zero failures.

(2) Build. Remaining at that snapshot: 115,199 modules.
- Measured rates: 3,071 per hour for the first 5.72 hours of the 8-job run; 2,669 per hour over the next 13.49 hours; 2,908 per hour in the last 15 minutes. The rate fell about 13 percent as depth grew.
- Derived: the remaining modules import 4,229 other project modules on average (tree mean 3,086, compiled so far 892).
- Projection, CPU-bound: 40 hours at the last 15-minute rate, 43 hours at 2,669 per hour. A linear fit of time per module against import closure gives about 1,890 per hour and 61 hours. The segment closure means behind that fit (300 and 1,250) are my assumption; the snapshots do not record them.
- The cloud pilot cannot settle the top of the graph. It never compiled above 17,860 imports and never read from disk (cloud-notes 8.1, 8.4). About 3.3 percent of the tree (about 5,800 modules) is above 17,860; 27 modules are above 50,000 and 13 above 100,000. The last modules each touch about 104 GiB and map about 130 GB of compiled files, against 24 GB of memory.
- On the evidence side, the Mac has already compiled a module importing 34,926 others while holding 2,908 per hour. Against that, a memory squeeze once cut the rate to 914 per hour (tuning.tsv, cap 7).
- My build range: 40 hours (floor) / about 60-75 hours (central) / 150 hours or more (high: jobs cut to 1-2 for the deepest few thousand modules, and paging). There is a non-zero chance the last 5 modules (closures 151,285 to 175,186) cannot finish on 24 GB at all.

(3) Kernel replay (C3). It has to run after the build: the scripts/09_kernel_replay.sh header (lines 47-50) says results that count should come from a run made after the build has finished. So the 36 closure-directory checks already done do not count, and the replay cannot overlap the build.
- Measured, with the build running at 8 jobs and the replay at 2: 17.5 and 23.8 seconds mean per leanchecker process (longest 95 and 91), and 11.5 to 18.2 seconds of wall time per module overall. By hand: 10-18 seconds, plus 0.5 ms per hard link made.
- Derived: at the tree's mean closure of 3,086, about 21-27 seconds per check including links. Over the whole tree that is about 1,000-1,300 process-hours, and 540.6 million hard links to make and remove (about 75 hours of link-making alone at 0.5 ms each).
- Projection: 21-28 days at 2 jobs at the measured busy-machine speed. About 14-18 days with three effective parallel checks. About 4-5.5 days only if an idle Mac runs checks twice as fast with five effective parallel jobs, and neither of those assumptions has been measured.
- Memory: private memory is probably enough (the Linux fit projects 2.7 GiB for the last module). But the deepest checks map about 100 GiB on 24 GB, so they will page from the SSD. kern.maxvnodes is 263,168 against about 240,000 mapped files projected for the last modules (430,000 by the pilot's regression). Raising it is a sudo sysctl, a system setting the owner must change himself.

(4) Disk is not a constraint. Free space was 3,177 GB at the last snapshot. The build writes about 1.4 TB in all (1.26 TB of it regenerable setup JSON). About 950 GB more is projected, leaving about 2.2 TB free with nothing pruned. Pruning the setup files would cut the build to about 150 GB.

(5) Risks are below.

Total calendar from the 15:31Z snapshot on 2026-11-21: about 6 days at best (around 2026-11-27); about 15-18 days central (around 2026-12-07); about 5 weeks or more at worst (late December), and possibly INCONCLUSIVE if the top modules cannot be built in 24 GB.

Cost: 0 USD in the cloud, so the total stays at no more than 11.53 USD. Electricity is a few dollars at most; that is my estimate, not measured.

analysis.verdict: The Mac can meet all of C1, C2 and C3 under the pre-registration as written, at no added cost: the cloud total stays at or below 11.53 USD. The price is time, plus one platform only (S3 deferred). The build is about 40-75 hours from the 15:31Z snapshot and could take 150 hours or more. The cost of removing links has never been timed.

The serial tail: 137 modules at depth 161-220 and a longest chain of 203 (performance-notes section 5) run largely one after another. check.assessment:
The core of the analysis holds, checked against the files. I verified the PREREGISTRATION.md quotations: line 66 lets the machine, OS and job count vary; C1 (line 48), C2 (lines 50-56) and C3 (line 60) name no machine; line 70 covers memory kills and line 84 gives INCONCLUSIVE; S3 is line 107. So C1-C3 can be met on the Mac alone, at no cloud cost, and Option D fits the 50 USD cap. The snapshot figures also check out: 59,988 of 175,187 compiled at 2026-11-21 15:31Z; the 8-job run started 2026-11-20 14:18; first START 10:18; zero failures. So do the rates (3,071/h, 2,669/h, last 15 minutes 2,908/h), the remaining-module mean closure of 4,229 (my recomputation from tree mean 3,086 and compiled mean 892), the disk arithmetic (247 GB over 36,007 modules, about 950 GB more, about 2.2 TB left free), the 540.6 million hard links, the 104 GiB touched and 2.7 GiB private memory projections (cloud-notes 8.1), and the 27 modules above 50,000 imports and 13 above 100,000 (cloud-notes 8.4).

Where it is wrong or short:
(1) The replay at the measured 2-job rate takes about 27-40 days, not 21-28. The script runs' wall time per module (11.5 and 18.3 s) already includes overhead that process seconds leave out. So the worst-case total is about 7 weeks or more (early January 2027), not 5. The central figure is unmeasured either way: replay scaling past 2 jobs on an idle Mac has never been timed. A short timed trial after the build is the only way to narrow a range of about 4-40 days.
(2) If the top of the graph cannot be built on 24 GB, there is no recovery within the owner's decisions and the cap. The branch ends INCONCLUSIVE. On macOS that is more likely to show up as very slow paging from the external SSD than as a clean memory kill.
(3) The --c3 run must start from an empty results file. Otherwise passes recorded while the build was running are silently reused, against the script's own rule.
(4) Swap on macOS grows on its own (3,072 MB at the first snapshot, 4,096 MB at the second). The real memory risk is file-backed .olean pages re-read from the SSD, together with the system-wide vnode limit (263,168 against about 236,000-434,000 mapped files at the top), which only the owner can raise and which resets on every restart.
(5) The 61 h central build figure rests on assumed segment closures, so it is a projection, not a measurement. Build floor about 40 h; central about 60-75 h plus an unmeasured serial, paging-bound tail of 137 deep modules; high 150 h or more.

Measured: snapshot counts, rates, disk, and the replay timings of 36 checks on a busy Mac. Projected: everything above 34,926 imports, replay scaling, the C2 time on Main. Unknown: whether macOS copes near the vnode limit, the boot-volume space available for swap, the cost of removing links, and the SSD's throughput under page faults.
